data.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet for AI purchases through retailer checkouts
data.description:
OpenAI is giving its artificial intelligence (AI) shopping agents a way to pay through retailers’ checkout systems, marking another shift in the ChatGPT maker’s evolving agentic commerce strategy.

Launched Nov. 13 in partnership with American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa, ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s “always-on” personal agents, known as dots, complete purchases on shoppers’ behalf.

Rather than keeping transactions inside ChatGPT, the virtual wallet works through merchants’ existing checkouts. Businesses retain their customer relationships, along with “control over pricing, fulfillment, returns, and customer service,” OpenAI said in its announcement.

For now, Wallet is rolling out to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers. While shoppers can add a payment card for agents to use, they must still approve each purchase before a transaction can be completed. The company has yet to identify any specific retailers accepting ChatGPT Wallet transactions.

Alongside the launch, OpenAI also released a Commerce Partner Playbook aimed at helping businesses prepare for a future of more agent-led purchases.

How ChatGPT Wallet works

The launch follows a change in OpenAI’s checkout plans earlier this year. After introducing Instant Checkout in September 2025, the company shifted toward transactions through merchant apps in March.

ChatGPT Wallet builds on that approach. “We’re building agent-led commerce to fit reliably into existing systems,” OpenAI said in its announcement.

According to the company, roughly 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week, including consumers researching and comparing products. Wallet aims to take that shopping activity a step further, allowing agents to complete purchases, it said.

Before checkout, shoppers review the items, total and payment card. They then authorize the purchase through a security check, such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan.

Once approved, the payment network generates a tokenized credential in place of the customer’s actual card details. Neither the merchant nor the AI agent receives those credentials, OpenAI said.

“Users keep their card’s existing rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, for example when an item is defective,” the company added. Banks and payment networks, meanwhile, continue evaluating transactions.

By starting with a limited rollout, OpenAI said it hopes to “learn from real-world use” and improve compatibility with businesses and payment providers.

Eventually, the company expects users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agents, with limits on spending, product categories or time periods. OpenAI said those transactions would still require “enhanced safeguards,” including biometric checks and records of authorization.

What ChatGPT Wallet means for online retailers

Keeping checkout in retailers’ hands may address one concern about agentic commerce. But that doesn’t mean every business is ready — or willing — to accept purchases made by AI agents.

Amazon, for example, blocked Meta’s Muse AI agent from shopping on its website in September, citing unauthorized activity and privacy and security concerns.

Other retailers may block legitimate transactions unintentionally. OpenAI acknowledged that existing security and fraud prevention systems can interfere with agent-led purchases.

Its new Commerce Partner Playbook offers guidance on making products accessible to agents and supporting payments through existing systems.

For starters, retailers can claim and verify their businesses in ChatGPT, then provide current product information, including pricing and availability.

But making products discoverable doesn’t guarantee agents can access a website. Retailers may need to configure their content delivery networks (CDNs) or firewalls to recognize signed requests through Web Bot Auth, a method for verifying AI agent identities. According to OpenAI, browser access doesn’t require a plugin or product feed.

Payment acceptance presents another hurdle. Fraud detection tools may flag legitimate agent purchases, leading to declined or canceled transactions.

To reduce those risks, OpenAI said it is working with payment providers Adyen, Checkout.com and Stripe, along with fraud prevention companies Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd.

Merchants can also add WebMCP tools or plugins to “let agents check availability, manage carts, or take other actions” through existing systems, the company said.

Payment companies expand their agentic commerce efforts

ChatGPT Wallet arrives as payment networks develop their own tools for AI-initiated transactions.

In April, Visa introduced Intelligent Commerce Connect, offering businesses a single integration for agent-led transactions. It followed in June with a partnership to bring Visa’s payment capabilities into OpenAI experiences.

Mastercard, meanwhile, introduced Agent Connect in September to connect merchants with AI agents, digital platforms and payment providers.

The push extends beyond consumer shopping. In October, Visa, BILL and Billtrust launched a live pilot enabling authorized AI agents to complete approved invoice payments through supplier portals.

data.title: Asics uses AI-powered drones to recover misplaced inventory 60% faster
data.description:
Asics America Corp. is using autonomous drones to find misplaced merchandise at its primary North American distribution center, a move the company says is helping it curb the risk of unfulfilled orders.

The technology, developed by Corvus Robotics, is helping the sportswear brand recover misplaced inventory about 60% faster, according to a Nov. 10 announcement from the warehouse automation provider.

At Asics’ facility in Byhalia, Mississippi, drones now conduct inventory counts in two key storage areas every month, up from twice annually. The higher frequency lets Asics offer merchandise on online marketplaces that were previously withheld due to fulfillment concerns.

Asics America, based in Irvine, California, is the U.S. subsidiary of Japanese sportswear company Asics Corp.

How Asics uses drones to count warehouse inventory

Asics’ 855,000-square-foot distribution center in Byhalia houses nearly 3 million units of footwear, apparel and accessories across roughly 44,000 stock-keeping units.

The facility fulfills ecommerce orders while also supplying Asics stores and wholesale customers. All three channels draw from the same inventory pool, and customer returns are processed there as well.

Asics is using Corvus One drones in two warehouse zones: a singles area that stores returned merchandise and individual pairs of shoes, and a case reserve area that holds full cartons.

The drones perform seven scheduled flights a night, starting at around 7 p.m., Corvus said. Using onboard computer vision and spatial reasoning, they navigate aisles less than 6 feet wide without needing additional warehouse infrastructure, such as markers or beacons.

During each flight, the drones scan universal product codes while also counting boxes stored at each location. Corvus said the system compares those counts with barcode scans, identifying inventory discrepancies. The following morning, a warehouse employee reviews the results using images and video captured during the flights.

“Now we can just look at the footage and we can tell exactly what’s going on with it in the locations before we have to send someone out,” Angela Williford, inventory control operations manager at Asics America, said in a Corvus video case study. “If it’s something that we can correct from the desk, we’ll correct it then.”

More frequent counts help Asics recover merchandise

During one three-month period, drones identified 26 misplaced cases containing more than 200 pairs of shoes. Without the additional counts, those items could have remained unavailable for sale until the next scheduled inventory review, Asics said.

Koestler estimated that Asics is recovering misplaced inventory roughly 60% faster than before the deployment.

“You don’t want to have to count a thousand locations to find the four or five that have problems,” he said in the video case study.

The automation has also shifted how warehouse employees spend their time. Rather than focusing on routine cycle counts, workers can dedicate more effort to inventory reconciliation, discrepancy investigations and wholesale-support projects, according to the companies.

Corvus also said the drones reduce the need for lift equipment during inventory counts, limiting traffic in the facility’s narrow aisles.

Asics makes more inventory available to marketplaces

The inventory gains have also influenced how Asics sells products through online marketplaces.

Before adopting the drone system, Asics withheld between 12 and 15 units out of every 100 from the inventory feeds it provided to marketplace partners, according to Corvus. The company did so because products shown as available might be missing or difficult to locate when orders arrived.

With monthly counts providing greater visibility into stock levels, Asics said it now publishes its full inventory availability feed.

Corvus said the change allows Asics to offer more merchandise at full price rather than potentially liquidating it at a discount. The companies did not disclose how much additional revenue the change has generated.

Other retailers expand warehouse automation

Asics is among a growing number of companies deploying inventory drones to improve warehouse operations.

After deploying Corvus’ technology, health and wellness retailer GNC increased inventory counts at its distribution centers in Indianapolis and Phoenix, according to a case study. Counts rose to as many as 10 to 12 times per year, up from two to four.

Likewise, Southern Glazer’s Wine & Spirits expanded its drone deployment to nine distribution centers. The beverage distributor reported a 100-basis-point improvement in cases handled per hour, Corvus said.

Other major retailers are investing in different forms of warehouse automation. Walmart Inc. recently announced plans to expand Symbotic automation technology across 25 U.S. regional distribution centers. The retailer said the rollout is designed to support inventory management, increase storage capacity and improve product flow throughout its supply chain.

data.title: J. Crew turns to Claude to create new Style Advisor tool
data.description:

data.title: Gap Q3 earnings: Online sales rise 3% as holiday outlook weakens
data.description:
Gap Inc.’s namesake brand continued its turnaround in fiscal Q3 2026, helping offset weaker performance elsewhere across its portfolio. Even so, the retailer lowered its full-year outlook after unseasonably warm weather slowed demand for fall apparel, executives said.

In its fiscal third quarter ended Oct. 31, Gap Inc. reported net sales of $4.01 billion, up 2% year over year. Online sales rose 3%, outpacing 1% growth in store sales. Ecommerce accounted for 40% of quarterly revenue, which was unchanged from a year earlier.

Performance varied widely across Gap Inc.’s four major brands. During Q3, its namesake Gap banner posted double-digit sales growth, while Old Navy’s comparable sales stabilized after declining in the prior quarter. Banana Republic reported a 3% year-over-year sales decline.

Athleta faced steeper losses in Q3, prompting Gap to appoint Ashley Kechter as the activewear brand’s next president and CEO, effective Dec. 14. Kechter most recently served as global president of Vuori and previously held leadership roles across Gap Inc.’s portfolio, including Banana Republic, Old Navy and Gap.

“Ashley grew up in the company and understands our culture and what it takes to operate at scale,” CEO Richard Dickson said on the earnings call.

On a positive note, executives said sales trends have improved as temperatures cooled. Gap also expects lower-than-previously-assumed U.S. tariff rates to add roughly $46 million to operating profit this year.

Gap Inc. ranks No. 19 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 2000 Database, which tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales and more.

The company is also No. 577 in Digital Commerce 360 and ReFiBuy’s AI Commerce Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

Gap Inc. web sales by year

Vuori ranks No. 558 in the Top 2000 and No. 332 in the AI Commerce Rankings.

Gap brand continues turnaround

Gap Inc.’s comparable sales, which include ecommerce, were flat year over year in its fiscal Q3 2026. Adjusted earnings per share increased 32% to $0.82, according to the company’s earnings release.

Reported net income in Q3 rose to $311 million, up from $236 million a year earlier.

Across its banners, the namesake Gap brand posted the strongest gains. Net sales rose 11% year over year to $1.06 billion, driven by denim and fleece. Comparable sales rose 9%, marking the brand’s 12th consecutive quarter of growth, Dickson said.

Old Navy, Gap Inc.’s largest brand, also showed signs of improvement. Net sales increased 1% to $2.27 billion, accounting for more than half of the company’s quarterly revenue. Comparable sales were flat after declining 4% in Q2.

Dickson credited stronger fall assortments — particularly denim, activewear and knits — along with more focused marketing and pricing changes aimed at improving value for shoppers.

In November, Michael Francis assumed the role of Old Navy president and CEO after serving as the brand’s chief customer officer.

“His deep engagement and stewardship over the past several months, particularly across marketing and merchandising, has been impactful in Q3,” Dickson said.

Banana Republic, Athleta face challenges

Banana Republic, meanwhile, reported a 3% decline in both net sales and comparable sales in Q3. Dickson attributed the weakness in part to softer demand for women’s apparel.

“First, the assortment was overweighted towards cold weather categories, including sweaters and outerwear, amid warmer-than-expected temperatures, particularly in October,” he said. “Second, we didn’t get the fashion and color point of view right in parts of the women’s assortment.”

Athleta’s net sales fell 14% year over year to $220 million, while comparable sales dropped 15%. Dickson acknowledged that efforts to modernize the brand’s assortment and marketing had fallen short amid growing competition.

“There’s new entrants reshaping the competitive landscape, and it is raising the bar for innovation, speed and relevance,” he said.

The company is now conducting a comprehensive review of Athleta, Dickson said.

Gap advances AI and digital engagement

Dickson said Gap Inc. remains the largest specialty apparel ecommerce business in the U.S. Its digital properties generated roughly 1.6 billion visits over the past 12 months, he said.

“We continue to advance our digital and app capabilities, including agentic commerce and, of course, always exploring emerging platforms like TikTok,” Dickson said.

Gap Inc. announced new AI shopping initiatives in October, including conversational product-discovery tools for Old Navy and Banana Republic. The retailer also partnered with Alta Daily to incorporate Gap merchandise into the styling app’s AI-generated outfit recommendations.

Gap is also using marketing partnerships to drive digital engagement.

Dickson said Old Navy’s back-to-school campaign with YouTube star MrBeast generated 1.4 billion global YouTube impressions, helping drive a more than 20% increase in traffic to its online children’s assortment. Dickson said Old Navy’s fall campaign with Cardi B also helped drive traffic while promoting its denim and cardigan assortments.

The company continues to update its physical footprint as well. Gap plans to remodel 35 Gap locations this year, bringing roughly a quarter of the brand’s North American specialty-store fleet into its latest format.

“The new Gap formats are outperforming their districts with really encouraging traffic and AUR (average unit retail) trends,” Dickson said.

Gap looks beyond apparel for growth

During Q3, Old Navy rolled out its beauty assortment nationwide. Dickson said customers purchasing beauty products are shopping across more of the store, with larger baskets and higher average transaction values than non-beauty shoppers.

The retailer is also seeing early momentum in accessories.

The Gap brand launched its first handbag collection in September. Dickson said several handbag styles sold out quickly, including the Five Pocket Tote, prompting the company to seek additional inventory.

Gap plans to introduce more handbag styles for the holiday season and expand its accessories offerings at Banana Republic and Old Navy in 2027. However, Dickson said they are not expected to make a meaningful financial contribution this year.

To further drive incremental sales, the company is also using licensing partnerships. Dickson said more than 60% of Old Navy shoppers who bought Fanatics merchandise also purchased products from the brand’s core apparel assortment, with baskets exceeding Old Navy’s average.

Gap lowers full-year outlook

Gap Inc. now expects fiscal 2026 revenue to be roughly flat year over year, down from its previous growth forecast of 1% to 1.5%.

Executives cited a slower-than-expected start to the holiday quarter. Old Navy increased promotions to attract shoppers, while Athleta stepped up discounting amid weaker sales.

Still, lower-than-expected U.S. tariff rates are projected to add roughly $46 million to Gap’s full-year operating profit, partially offsetting other pressures on the business. The retailer ended Q3 with $2.3 billion in inventory, down 6% from a year earlier.

Separately, Gap recorded a $420 million year-to-date adjustment to cost of goods sold related to the recovery of tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). It also recorded $21 million in related interest income. The company excluded both benefits from its adjusted full-year outlook.

Percentage changes may not align exactly with dollar figures due to rounding. Check back for more earnings reports. Here’s last quarter’s update on Gap revenue.

data.title: Williams-Sonoma ecommerce sales rise 6.8% as every brand posts comparable growth in Q3
data.description:
Williams-Sonoma Inc. grew ecommerce sales for a fourth consecutive quarter in its fiscal Q3 2026, as every brand and channel posted positive comparable sales. 

Net revenue for the quarter ended Nov. 1 rose 5.8% year over year to $1.99 billion. Comparable brand revenue, which includes ecommerce, stores and business-to-business sales, increased 5.1%.

Ecommerce comparable sales grew 6.8%, CFO Jeff Howie said on an earnings call with investors. That compares with 6.5% in Q2. Retail comparable sales rose 1.5%, on top of 8.5% growth last year.

Williams-Sonoma is No. 22 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database, which ranks North America’s largest online retailers by annual ecommerce sales.

Williams-Sonoma is also No. 306 in Digital Commerce 360 and ReFiBuy’s AI Commerce Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

Williams-Sonoma web sales by year

Williams-Sonoma Q3 results by brand

  • West Elm: Comparable sales rose 7.0%, driven by furniture, nonfurniture and brand collaborations.
  • Williams Sonoma: Comparable sales grew 6.8%, with positive results in every division.
  • Pottery Barn Kids and Teen: Comparable sales rose 2.9%, helped by record furniture sales in its dorm business.
  • Pottery Barn: Comparable sales rose 1.8%, down from 5.1% in Q2.

In Q3, the retailer continued its initiative of leaning into full-price selling, which is weighing on Pottery Barn’s sales growth while lifting margins.

CEO Laura Alber said Pottery Barn’s slowdown was by design. The company cut markdowns on nonfurniture items, especially seasonal goods such as Halloween and back-to-school products.

“We knew this change would have an impact on the near term comp in the Pottery Barn brands, but we believe it is the right strategy for long term profitability,” she said.

The full-price approach is working on margins. Non-GAAP operating margin rose 40 basis points to 17.4%, and non-GAAP earnings per share grew 11.7% to $2.19. Alber said competitors are running deeper promotions, with some marking down as much as 70% of their assortments. Williams-Sonoma plans the same approach for Q4.

Williams-Sonoma expands AI across brands

Alber said the company’s artificial intelligence (AI) assistants have now supported more than 1 million customer chat visits. Revenue per visit for shoppers who engage with personalized experiences is “up substantially” versus the site average, she said. The retailer has Olive, an AI assistant on the Williams Sonoma website, and Otto, an assistant on the Pottery Barn website.

Chief digital officer Sameer Hassan described a design tool that turns a 3D plan of a customer’s room into a photorealistic image in seconds. It uses the actual products a customer selects, with real dimensions.

“This is an AI-guided complete design that you are seeing in your space, including decor, just something that is unparalleled in the industry,” Hassan said. For the holidays, the retailer will use AI-generated gifting imagery and send gift-giver reminders based on past purchases.

Diesel costs and delays add pressure

Rising fuel costs and supply chain disruption are the main pressures facing Williams-Sonoma. Howie said U.S. diesel prices were up more than 60% year over year in Q3 and 20% since August. The increase could add as much as $60 million in expense for the year.

Alber also cited longer transit times from the Middle East conflict, along with port and rail congestion. Williams-Sonoma is expediting key shipments and updating delivery estimates on its site. She said the housing market “has gotten worse,” even as the company gained share.

Tariffs were a smaller factor for the retailer. Williams-Sonoma recognized $29.3 million in IEEPA tariff refunds in Q3 and has collected substantially all of its $197.8 million claim.
